concepts.decision: Classify the attacker capability and target before selecting a mitigation.
concepts.definition: Analysis of cryptographic designs or implementations to find exploitable weaknesses.
concepts.failureExample: A response calls every credential attack “breaking encryption.”
concepts.label: Cryptanalysis

concepts.decision: Use adequate key strength and constrain online guesses with rate controls and monitoring.
concepts.definition: Repeated attempts to guess keys, passwords, or secrets.
concepts.failureExample: Unlimited login attempts make a weak password practical to guess.
concepts.label: Brute Force

concepts.decision: Use modern approved designs and avoid predictable weak historical patterns.
concepts.definition: Attack with ciphertext samples but no confirmed corresponding plaintext.
concepts.failureExample: A team relies on obscurity because attackers “only see encrypted data.”
concepts.label: Ciphertext Only Attack

concepts.decision: Avoid schemes or configurations whose security fails under known content.
concepts.definition: Attack where the adversary knows some plaintext-ciphertext pairs.
concepts.failureExample: Standard file headers give an attacker predictable plaintext pairs.
concepts.label: Known Plaintext Attack

concepts.decision: Avoid classical or pattern-leaking designs for modern protection.
concepts.definition: Use of predictable symbol or pattern distributions to attack weak or historical ciphers.
concepts.failureExample: A simple substitution scheme preserves letter frequency in sensitive messages.
concepts.label: Frequency Analysis

concepts.decision: Use authenticated modern protocols, strict state/input validation, and nonrevealing errors.
concepts.definition: Attack where selected ciphertexts are submitted to a decryption-related behavior and outputs reveal information.
concepts.failureExample: A service reveals different messages for padding or decryption failures.
concepts.label: Chosen Ciphertext Attack

concepts.decision: Select approved key sizes and protect against implementation or online-guess shortcuts.
concepts.definition: Set of possible key values that determines search difficulty with other attack factors.
concepts.failureExample: A nominally strong algorithm uses a small or reused secret.
concepts.label: Key Space

concepts.decision: Validate before acting and reject malformed, replayed, downgraded, or inconsistent states.
concepts.definition: Checking message, parameter, identity, state, and error conditions in a cryptographic protocol.
concepts.failureExample: A protocol accepts an unauthenticated downgrade to an older mode.
concepts.label: Protocol Validation

concepts.decision: Tune by account, source, service, availability, and monitoring requirements.
concepts.definition: Constraint on repeated attempts to reduce online guessing and abuse.
concepts.failureExample: An attacker makes thousands of password guesses because the endpoint never slows or alerts.
concepts.label: Rate Limiting

misconceptions.claim: Any encryption makes frequency analysis irrelevant.
misconceptions.correction: Modern approved mechanisms are designed differently from simple substitution systems, but security still depends on correct algorithm, mode or protocol, keys, inputs, and implementation.

outcome: Distinguish brute-force, ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, frequency-analysis, and chosen-ciphertext assumptions and match each to a mitigation category.

sections.body: A brute-force attack attempts candidate keys or credentials until one succeeds, so effective key strength, rate limits, authentication controls, and detection matter. A ciphertext-only attack gives the adversary ciphertexts but no confirmed corresponding plaintext. A known-plaintext attack assumes some plaintext-ciphertext pairs are known. Frequency analysis exploits predictable symbol or pattern distribution, particularly in weak or historical designs. Chosen-ciphertext reasoning assumes an attacker can submit selected ciphertexts to a decryption-related behavior and learn from outputs or errors.
keyPoints: Attack labels describe assumptions, not automatic success.
The same system can expose multiple attacker capabilities.
sections.title: Model the information and control available to the adversary

sections.body: Use approved modern cryptography and adequate key strength rather than relying on obscurity or historical patterns. Protect keys and credentials; constrain online guesses with rate, lockout, and monitoring appropriate to the use case; avoid error behavior that creates a decryption oracle; validate inputs and protocol state; and keep libraries and configurations current. Do not assume that encryption alone eliminates replay, downgrade, identity, or endpoint risks. Mitigation must match the actual protocol and threat model.
keyPoints: Rate limiting addresses an online guessing path; it does not repair weak cryptographic construction.
Generic errors and correct protocol validation can prevent attackers from learning through different responses.
sections.title: Reduce capability through sound design and operation

sections.body: Document the cryptographic profile, keys and their lifecycle, protocol state machine, expected failures, monitoring signals, and update authority. Test known failure conditions in authorized environments: malformed input, expired credentials, repeated requests, protocol downgrade attempts, and response consistency. Use approved tools and scope because decryption-oracle or high-rate testing against production can itself create availability or disclosure risk. Feed findings to design, key-management, and incident processes.
keyPoints: Security testing must be authorized and designed not to become an attack.
Evidence links a threat assumption to a tested control behavior.

summary: Cryptanalytic attack labels describe what an adversary can observe, obtain, choose, or compute. Brute-force, ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, frequency-analysis, and chosen-ciphertext reasoning helps an architect avoid claims that a mechanism is safe without considering keys, inputs, protocols, and implementation behavior.

assumptions: Only entities and claims anchored in the canonical unit or explicitly labeled hypothetical scenario are used.
A highlighted path means the learner is inspecting that path; it does not assert the event occurred.
The current source is authoritative for facts; this treatment reorganizes presentation without changing canonical content.
The lesson teaches one bounded decision and does not claim to exhaust every jurisdiction, vendor implementation, architecture, attack, or exception.
teaching.focalRelation: Brute force searches key space; ciphertext-only and known-plaintext supply different observations; frequency analysis depends on structure; chosen-ciphertext adds controlled inputs and observable responses; rate limiting applies only to applicable online paths.
